title: The first images
hookLine: in Gandhara and Mathura, the first statues of the Buddha appear

cards: Two statues stand in a museum, a few steps apart. Both are the Buddha.
The first is carved in gray stone: wavy hair, a calm face, a heavy robe falling in deep folds over both shoulders, a body that looks as if it could breathe.
The second is reddish stone: a rounder face, broad shoulders, one shoulder bare, a slight smile, a hand raised with the palm out. They come from two different regions, Gandhara and Mathura.
After the empty seat, the Buddha has a face. In fact, he has two.

teach.b: First, Gandhara. In the northwest, where trade roads crossed and many peoples met, carvers made Buddhas with flowing hair and robes in deep, rippling folds.
Art historians see in them the touch of Greek and Roman sculpture, which had reached that region. The Buddha stands like a figure from a classical temple, but his eyes are lowered, and he is still.
Second, Mathura. Further south and east, carvers in the city of Mathura worked in a reddish sandstone.
Their Buddhas are fuller, broad-chested, often smiling, in a thin robe that clings to the body: strong, present, ready to speak. Third, the question nobody can settle.
Which came first? Scholars have argued for a long time and still disagree. Some look to Gandhara, some to Mathura, and some think the two began around the same time.
It's honest to leave it open. Fourth, the signs that stayed.

teach.h: THE HAND THAT SAYS DO NOT FEAR.
teach.b: Whatever the style, the new images carried marks that meant something: a rise on the crown of the head, a small mark between the eyebrows, long earlobes, stretched, tradition says, by the heavy earrings of the prince he once was.

And one hand raised, palm out, in the gesture often read as do not fear. The empty seat had said: he is gone beyond measure. The statue says: he was here, and this is what a calm human being can look like.
Buddhist art goes on holding both. The images didn't replace the wheel and the footprint. They sat down beside them.

how: Buddhists today bow before images of the Buddha and offer flowers, candles and incense, and the wheel and footprint remain in use beside them.

a hand gesture that means do not fear

games.q: you're a carver in Gandhara. until now the Buddha has been shown by an empty seat. a patron asks you to carve him as a man. how do you show what he is?
o: make him look like a king in armor.
a calm figure, eyes lowered, with signs like the mark between the brows.
games.why: the new images show a calm figure, eyes lowered, carrying signs like the rise on the crown and the mark between the eyebrows.

practice: Find a picture of a Gandhara or Mathura Buddha, or bring to mind any image of the Buddha you've seen, and look slowly: the hands first, then the shoulders, then the eyes and the mouth, noticing what the carver chose to show.
Then close your eyes and see if any of that stillness can settle into your own face and hands.

wordCard.voice: Gandhara. The northwest region whose carvers gave the Buddha flowing hair and rippling robes, touched by Greek and Roman sculpture.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: buddha, the awakened one. the title, now carved with a face.
